summary.text: Assuming the first asserted identity, the shifted terms \(a_n+1\) satisfy a Fibonacci recurrence modulo \(195318521017\); a finite computation of the initial residues followed by binary matrix exponentiation shows that at \(K=249580073233\), two consecutive shifted residues are both \(1\), so the corresponding consecutive terms are divisible by the modulus. Their gcd is therefore greater than \(1\), making the defining recurrence’s next value strictly less than \(1+x+y\) and contradicting the asserted identity.

full_proof.text:
Let \((a_n)\) be the sequence in the question. Thus
\[
a_1=a_2=1,
\qquad
a_n=g_n+\frac{a_{n-1}+a_{n-2}}{g_n}\quad(n\geq 3),
\qquad
g_n=\gcd(a_{n-1},a_{n-2}).
\]
For convenience one may also put \(a_0=0\); this has no effect on any positive-indexed term.

We will disprove even the first asserted formula
\[
 a_n=1+a_{n-1}+a_{n-2}\qquad(n\geq3775).
\]
Consequently, the conjunction of the three formulas in the conjecture is false, regardless of the other two formulas.

We use the two integers
\[
p=195318521017,
\qquad
K=249580073233.
\]
No primality assertion about \(p\) is needed; only \(p>1\) will be used.

First, a direct finite calculation of the defining recurrence from the initial values up to indices \(3773\) and \(3774\) gives
\[
 a_{3773}+1\equiv 77940394259\pmod p,
\qquad
 a_{3774}+1\equiv 99768150822\pmod p. \tag{1}
\]
This computation is performed with the actual integer terms, not by trying to evaluate the recurrence solely modulo \(p\), since the gcd and the integer quotient depend on the full terms. More explicitly, it is the following finite tabulation: begin with
\[
A_0=0, quad A_1=A_2=1,
\]
and, successively for \(j=3,4,\ldots,3774\), calculate
\[
 d_j=\gcd(A_{j-1},A_{j-2}),
 \qquad
 A_j=d_j+\frac{A_{j-1}+A_{j-2}}{d_j}.
\]
The Euclidean algorithm supplies each gcd and exact integer division supplies the quotient. Reducing only the final two values plus one modulo \(195318521017\) gives
\[
(A_{3773}+1)\bmod p=77940394259,
\qquad
(A_{3774}+1)\bmod p=99768150822,
\]
which is (1). This is a finite calculation of 3772 applications of the displayed recurrence.

Now suppose, for contradiction, that the first formula in the conjecture holds for every \(n\geq3775\):
\[
 a_n=1+a_{n-1}+a_{n-2}. \tag{2}
\]
Introduce the shifted residues
\[
 u_k\equiv a_{3773+k}+1\pmod p\qquad(k\geq0).
\]
For every \(k\geq0\), equation (2), applied at index \(3775+k\), gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{3775+k}+1
 &=2+a_{3774+k}+a_{3773+k}\\
 &=(a_{3774+k}+1)+(a_{3773+k}+1).
\end{aligned}
\]
Therefore the shifted residues satisfy the ordinary Fibonacci recurrence
\[
 u_{k+2}=u_{k+1}+u_k\quad\text{in }\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z. \tag{3}
\]
By (1), their initial values are
\[
 u_0=77940394259,
\qquad
 u_1=99768150822
 \quad\text{in }\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z. \tag{4}
\]

We next evaluate this Fibonacci recurrence at the distant index \(K\). Put
\[
T=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Equation (3) implies, by induction on \(k\), that
\[
 \binom{u_{k+1}}{u_k}
 =T^k\binom{u_1}{u_0}
 \quad\text{in }(\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)^2. \tag{5}
\]
Indeed, the assertion is immediate for \(k=0\), and multiplication by \(T\) changes \((u_{k+1},u_k)^t\) into \((u_{k+1}+u_k,u_{k+1})^t=(u_{k+2},u_{k+1})^t\).

For completeness, here is the modular repeated-squaring calculation of the power in (5). The binary expansion of \(K\) is
\[
K=(11101000011100001000011011000100010001)_2.
\]
Reading these bits from left to right, if the exponent represented by the bits read so far is \(e\) and the corresponding matrix is \(T^e\), the next matrix is \((T^e)^2\) when the next bit is 0 and \(T(T^e)^2\) when it is 1. Thus
\[
T^K\equiv
\begin{pmatrix}
139205883321&21827756563\\
21827756563&117378126758
\end{pmatrix}\pmod p. \tag{6}
\]
Multiplying (6) by the initial vector in (4) gives
\[
\begin{pmatrix}
139205883321&21827756563\\
21827756563&117378126758
\end{pmatrix}
\binom{99768150822}{77940394259}
\equiv
\binom11\pmod p. \tag{7}
\]
Combining (5) and (7), we obtain
\[
 u_K=1,
\qquad
 u_{K+1}=1
 \quad\text{in }\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z. \tag{8}
\]
Recalling the definition of \(u_k\), equation (8) says
\[
 a_{3773+K}+1\equiv1\pmod p,
\qquad
 a_{3774+K}+1\equiv1\pmod p.
\]
Hence
\[
 p\mid a_{3773+K},
\qquad
 p\mid a_{3774+K}. \tag{9}
\]

We now compare the true defining recurrence with the conjectured recurrence at the next index.

First note that every \(a_n\) with \(n\geq1\) is positive. This follows by strong induction. It is true for \(a_1=a_2=1\). If the preceding terms are positive, their gcd is positive, and the defining formula expresses the next term as that positive gcd plus a nonnegative integer. In particular, set
\[
 x=a_{3774+K},
\qquad
 y=a_{3773+K},
\qquad
 g=\gcd(x,y).
\]
Then \(x,y>0\). By (9), \(p\) is a common divisor of \(x\) and \(y\), so \(p\mid g\). Since \(g>0\), this implies \(g\geq p>1\).

We need the following elementary inequality. If \(x,y>0\), \(g>1\), and \(g\) divides both \(x\) and \(y\), then
\[
 g+\frac{x+y}{g}<1+x+y. \tag{10}
\]
To prove it, write
\[
k=\frac{x+y}{g}.
\]
Because \(g\mid x,y\) and \(x,y>0\), both \(x\) and \(y\) are at least \(g\). Consequently \(x+y\geq2g\), so \(k\geq2\). Also \(x+y=gk\). Therefore
\[
(1+x+y)-(g+k)
 =1+gk-g-k
 =(g-1)(k-1)>0,
\]
which proves (10).

Apply the actual defining recurrence at index
\[
N=3775+K=249580077008.
\]
Its two preceding terms are precisely \(x=a_{3774+K}\) and \(y=a_{3773+K}\), and their gcd is \(g\). Thus
\[
 a_N=g+\frac{x+y}{g}. \tag{11}
\]
Since \(g>1\), inequality (10) and (11) give
\[
 a_N<1+x+y. \tag{12}
\]
On the other hand, \(N\geq3775\), so the assumed conjectural identity (2), applied at \(N\), gives
\[
 a_N=1+a_{N-1}+a_{N-2}=1+x+y, \tag{13}
\]
contradicting (12).

Therefore it is impossible that
\[
a_n=1+a_{n-1}+a_{n-2}
\]
holds for every \(n\geq3775\). Since the stated OEIS conjecture asserts this identity together with two further identities for every such \(n\), the full three-part conjecture is false.
